When I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set, surface-form variation was a systematic confounder [lib:cv]; van Schijndel's probing methodology for separating orthographic from semantic representations offers a principled way to study the same phenomenon in Indian scripts. His broader focus on syntax and semantics across languages [advisor:Marten van Schijndel] aligns with my goal of building evaluations that go beyond translated English benchmarks [lib:interests].

Prof. Koenecke's work documenting how speech-to-text systems produce hallucinations that cause concrete harms [paper:W4391833135] frames exactly the reliability question I encountered when training a wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio [lib:cv]. Her research on ASR failure modes and dialect disparities [advisor:Allison Koenecke] maps onto the challenge of building trustworthy speech-text pipelines for Indian languages where labelled written data is scarce [lib:interests]. I want to extend that failure-mode analysis to low-resource, spoken-language-dominant settings where the consequences of hallucination are especially high.

Prof. Artzi's research on LLM post-training, including in-context reinforcement learning from bandit feedback [paper:W4403346162], connects to my interest in data-efficient adaptation of LLMs to Indian languages [lib:interests]. Learning effectively from scarce or indirect supervision is central to low-resource settings, and that framing aligns with the adaptation challenges I studied during my tokenizer work at Microsoft Research India [lib:cv]. Prof. Artzi's lab also works on LLM evaluation methodology [advisor:Yoav Artzi], which directly addresses my second research direction: building evaluations that measure code-switching and cultural grounding rather than relying on translated English benchmarks [lib:interests].

sop.text:
I am applying to the PhD program in Computer Science to work on multilingual natural language processing—specifically, making large language models useful for the hundreds of millions of people who speak Indian languages but are poorly served by today's systems.

My interest comes from a concrete failure. In 2025 I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set of 2,400 sentences and found that two open 7B models lost 18–26 points compared with monolingual Tamil inputs [lib:cv]. People in Chennai do not speak monolingual Tamil to a chatbot; they switch. That result became my first-author workshop paper at an ACL-family conference [lib:cv] and convinced me that evaluation—not just training—is where multilingual NLP is broken.

At Microsoft Research India in summer 2026, mentored by Dr. Anjali Mehra, I worked on the other side of the problem: adaptation [lib:cv]. Extending a sentencepiece vocabulary with 6,000 Kannada tokens cut average tokens per sentence by 41% and improved downstream QA F1 by 3.4 points at the same fine-tuning budget [lib:cv]. The lesson was that cheap, targeted changes to the tokenizer can matter as much as expensive fine-tuning—a principle I want to study more rigorously in a PhD.

In a separate course project I trained a wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio, achieving 31% WER on a held-out set [lib:cv]. That experiment surfaced a harder question: for languages where text corpora are thin but speech is abundant, how do we build and evaluate speech-text models whose failure modes we actually understand?

These three threads define my PhD research plan: (1) parameter-efficient and data-efficient adaptation of LLMs to low-resource Indian languages, (2) evaluation frameworks that capture code-switching, cultural grounding, and faithfulness rather than relying on translated English benchmarks, and (3) robust speech-text models for languages whose data is primarily spoken.

At Cornell I am interested in working with Prof. Marten van Schijndel, whose probing work on contextual embeddings under orthographic noise [paper:W4402670872] and on Hindi syntactic structure [paper:W4396913907] offers methodological tools for the surface-variation problems I encountered in code-switched Tamil. I am also interested in Prof. Allison Koenecke, whose analysis of speech-to-text hallucination harms [paper:W4391833135] addresses the reliability questions raised by my Tamil speech project. Finally, Prof. Yoav Artzi's work on in-context learning from bandit feedback [paper:W4403346162] and his lab's focus on LLM evaluation [advisor:Yoav Artzi] connect to both my adaptation and evaluation interests.

I hold a CGPA of 9.21/10 (top 5% of my department) at NIT Tiruchirappalli [lib:profile]. I have served as a teaching assistant for a 120-student machine learning course and organise my department's NLP reading group, which now has approximately 25 members [lib:cv]. I have two confirmed research mentors—Prof. S. Venkatesan, who co-authored the workshop paper with me, and Dr. Anjali Mehra from Microsoft Research India—who will speak directly to my research trajectory [lib:recommenders].

Cornell's breadth across NLP, speech, and evaluation methodology, combined with the specific faculty above, makes it the right environment to pursue these questions at the intersection of linguistic diversity and model reliability.

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student interested in multilingual NLP and Hindi/Tamil syntactic evaluation
emails.body:
Dear Prof. van Schijndel,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to Cornell's CS PhD program for Fall 2027. My research focuses on evaluation and adaptation of LLMs for Indian languages.

I read your 2024 paper 'Does Dependency Locality Predict Non-canonical Word Order in Hindi?' [paper:W4396913907] with particular interest. The dependency-based framing connects closely to a problem I have been working on: I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set of 2,400 sentences and found that open 7B models lose 18–26 points relative to monolingual Tamil baselines [lib:cv]. Understanding what syntactic and structural features drive those failures seems like a natural extension of your approach.

I would be grateful to know whether you are planning to take PhD students for Fall 2027. I would be happy to share my CV and my workshop paper on Tamil–English code-switch robustness [lib:cv].

Thank you for your time.

Priya Raman
